section_summary: This section comprises U.S. Embassy Tokyo's monthly political reports and accompanying transmittal despatches for May, June, and July 1936 (Reports Nos. 116, 117, and 118), including schedules of despatches and telegrams sent to the Department of State. The documents record growing Sino-Japanese friction over illicit smuggling operations and the expansion of the Japanese garrison in North China, Soviet-Japanese border tension and fisheries negotiations, trade conflicts with Australia over textile and wool tariffs, and Japan's refusal to adhere to the 1936 London Naval Treaty. Domestically, they chronicle the political and judicial aftermath of the February 26 Incident, including the courts martial and execution of the young officer insurgents and Lieutenant Colonel Aizawa, the lifting of martial law in Tokyo, the entrenchment of military control over national policy, and economic legislation such as the Automobile Industry Control Law.

subfiles.about: Embassy monthly political report on foreign relations, domestic politics, and economic conditions in Japan during May 1936.
subfiles.summary: The concluding section of the Embassy's report for May 1936 reviews Japan's increasing military presence in North China and the growing diplomatic friction caused by rampant Japanese smuggling operations in China. In foreign affairs, it notes Soviet-Japanese border matters, a provisional fisheries treaty extension, British naval intentions, and retaliatory trade friction with Australia over textile tariffs. Domestically, the report details debates in the 69th Diet session criticizing the military, Imperial Ordinances restricting service ministers to active-duty officers, passage of the Automobile Industry Control Law, and government finances, concluding with lists of despatches and telegrams sent to Washington during May 1936.
subfiles.title: Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of May, 1936 (Report No. 116)

subfiles.about: Embassy Despatch No. 1942 transmitting Report No. 117 on political, diplomatic, and economic conditions in Japan during June 1936.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits Report No. 117 reviewing political, diplomatic, and economic developments in Japan during June 1936. International topics include negotiations with foreign oil companies under the Petroleum Industry Law, the visit of Admiral Murfin on the USS Augusta, unchecked smuggling in North China, Japan's formal refusal to adhere to the London Naval Treaty of 1936, the second visit of Sir Frederick Leith-Ross, retaliatory trade measures against Australia under the Trade Protection Law, and a treaty abolishing Japanese extraterritoriality in Manchukuo. On domestic matters, the report details ongoing military trials of the February 26 insurgents, Army dominance over Cabinet administrative reform proposals, and increased defense spending, followed by a list of despatches forwarded in June.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1942: Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of June, 1936 (Report No. 117)

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch transmitting Report No. 118 on political, diplomatic, and economic conditions in Japan during July 1936.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits Report No. 118 detailing conditions in Japan during July 1936. The diplomatic section covers American oil negotiations, Japanese alarm over rumored Western financial and munitions loans to China, trade parleys with Australia, Japan's signature of the Montreux Treaty regarding the Dardanelles, and the entry into force of the Manchukuo extraterritoriality treaty. Domestically, the report records the execution of Lieutenant Colonel Saburo Aizawa and fifteen participants in the February 26 Incident, the lifting of martial law in Tokyo, the sentencing of Captain Yamaguchi, creation of a unified Army Air Force Headquarters, a massive twenty-year emigration program to Manchuria, enforcement of the Automobile Manufacturing Industry Law, and a list of July despatches.
subfiles.title: Despatch transmitting Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of July, 1936 (Report No. 118)
